issues.legal_issue: Street vending on public streets is a protected form of business, but it does not confer an unrestricted right to trade or occupy a particular spot.
material_facts: The proceedings concerned street hawkers and vendors seeking to carry on business on public streets.
Earlier decisions considered in the judgment had recognized street vending as a fundamental right while subjecting it to regulation and the rights of other street users.
issues.conclusion: The Court affirmed that street vending is protected under Article 19(1)(g), subject to reasonable restrictions, and does not give a vendor a right to occupy a particular place of choice regardless of others’ rights.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(g) protects the right to carry on street vending, subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(6). The Court relied on Sodan Singh v. New Delhi Municipal Committee, which recognized the right but rejected an unrestricted right to a particular pavement location, and Saudan Singh v. NDMC, which explained that the right does not extend to occupying a specific place regardless of the rights of others. The Court also noted the need to harmonize vendors’ rights with commuters’ rights under Article 19(1)(d).

predicates.public_street_vending_case: The proceeding concerns people seeking to trade as vendors on public streets.
predicates.street_vending_is_legitimate_trade: The vendors seek to earn their livelihood through street vending.

issues.definition: When a case concerns legitimate trading on public streets, the trading is protected subject to reasonable restrictions, but that protection does not include a right to a fixed spot.

issues.legal_issue: Restrictions on the fundamental right to street vending must be imposed by law and cannot be imposed solely through non-statutory schemes or policy.
material_facts: The municipal authorities had framed schemes to regulate hawking and vending, including schemes framed pursuant to a national policy and court directions.
The Court found that the schemes and policy did not have the status of law or subordinate legislation.
The Court found that no relevant vending-regulation bye-laws had been made under the municipal authority’s power to make them.
The municipal statutes contained certain provisions concerning permission, licensing, removal of obstructions and the power to make bye-laws.
issues.conclusion: Only existing or newly made law having statutory force may impose reasonable restrictions on the right to street vending; the schemes and policy alone were not law. The appropriate Government was directed to enact legislation to regulate street vending.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(g) is subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(6), but those restrictions must be imposed by existing law or law made by the State. The Court relied on Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala, which held that restrictions under Article 19 must be imposed by law having statutory force, and on the Constitution Bench decisions in Kameshwar Prasad v. State of Bihar and Kharak Singh v. State of U.P. The Court also relied on Sodan Singh v. New Delhi Municipal Committee concerning the protected right to hawk. It considered, among other provisions, Sections 320, 322 and 481 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, and Sections 225, 226, 330, 369(2), 388, 389 and 390 of the New Delhi Municipal Council Act, 1994, and found that the schemes and policy were not themselves law and that relevant bye-laws had not been made.

predicates.public_interest_street_vending_case: The proceeding concerns the regulation of street vending in the public interest.
predicates.hawking_restrictions_are_imposed_by_a_no: The authorities seek to regulate street vending through a scheme or policy that does not have statutory force.
predicates.no_statutory_vending_bye_laws_exist: The municipal authority has not made statutory bye-laws governing the relevant vending activity.

issues.definition: If street vending is being regulated in the public interest through a non-statutory scheme and no relevant statutory bye-laws exist, reasonable restrictions on vending require statutory law.

issues.legal_issue: Existing municipal vending schemes may continue as an interim means of regulation while legislation is being brought into force.
material_facts: The municipal authorities had existing schemes for regulating hawking and street vending.
The Court found that a statutory framework regulating street vending was still needed and directed the appropriate Government to enact one.
The proceedings involved an ongoing problem of regulating vending while that framework was absent.
issues.conclusion: The Court directed that the existing schemes could regulate hawking and street vending temporarily pending legislation.
issues.legal_principle: The Court’s interim direction preserved the operation of the existing municipal schemes while recognizing that they were not law and that legislation was necessary. The direction was made in the context of the Court’s earlier supervision of the schemes and its conclusion that the problem required a statutory framework.

predicates.public_interest_street_vending_case: The proceeding concerns regulation of street vending in the public interest.
predicates.legislation_is_not_yet_in_force: A statutory framework regulating the relevant street vending has not yet come into force.
predicates.existing_municipal_vending_schemes_are_o: Municipal authorities have schemes already operating to regulate street vending.

issues.definition: Where legislation is not yet in force and municipal vending schemes are operating in a public-interest street-vending case, those schemes may regulate vending temporarily pending legislation.

issues.legal_issue: Vendors must use the dispute-redressal mechanisms provided by the municipal schemes instead of bypassing them with a direct approach to the Supreme Court.
material_facts: The municipal authorities described multi-level dispute-redressal arrangements in their affidavits, including committees and appellate authorities.
The affidavits stated that decisions could be appealed through the specified levels and that decisions not appealed would be final at that level.
The Court directed vendors to abide by those mechanisms and noted that the schemes provided for redress of their grievances.
issues.conclusion: Vendors must pursue the dispute-redressal mechanisms in the schemes, and must not make a direct approach to the Supreme Court by a fresh petition or application that bypasses those mechanisms.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied its directions governing the municipal schemes and the dispute-redressal arrangements disclosed in the municipal authorities’ affidavits. It directed that grievances be addressed through those arrangements rather than by bypassing them with a direct approach to the Court.

predicates.street_vending_grievance_case: The proceeding concerns a grievance arising from the regulation or allocation of street vending.
predicates.the_scheme_provides_internal_dispute_red: The applicable vending scheme provides committees or other internal bodies to hear grievances and appeals.
predicates.the_grievance_falls_within_that_mechanis: The vendor’s grievance is of a kind that the scheme’s dispute-redressal arrangements can consider.

issues.definition: When a vending grievance is covered by an internal dispute mechanism provided in the scheme, that mechanism must be used before a direct approach to the Supreme Court.
